archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A short-area passer whose legs have always been the separator. In Minnesota he is being used almost purely as a scrambler (six scrambles, one designed run) inside a conservative, run-leaning game plan.

report.headline: Accurate enough, sacked too often: a defense-carried 2-0 hides a stalled passing game
report.take:
Murray arrives in Minnesota as an eight-year veteran with a stable profile. He has been a quick-game passer with an aDOT between 6 and 8 every season. In four of his first six years he ranked second to fourth among QBs in rushing yards. He has never avoided sacks well: his pressure-to-sack rate ranked 27th or worse every season, and it bottomed out at 0.50 in a five-game 2025. Under Kevin O'Connell the role is narrower. Minnesota passes 5 points less than situation predicts (24th), and it owns the league's best defense by EPA, success rate and sack rate. His job so far has been to not lose games, and the 2-0 record says that is all he has had to do.

The -0.221 EPA per dropback (38th of 42) looks like a broken quarterback. Split it apart and the picture changes. His 54 throws at or beyond the line work out to roughly +0.11 EPA per attempt, and the intermediate and deep balls are both above +0.26. The damage comes from two places. First, 17 throws behind the line of scrimmage have produced -0.616 per play with an 11.8% success rate. Second, seven sacks on 84 dropbacks are what really sink the number. The line isn't the main cause yet: he has been pressured on only 14.9% of dropbacks, fourth-lowest in the league. His 2.96-second time to throw is slower than any season of his career, so he is holding clean pockets too long. Four of the seven sacks came on third down, where Minnesota converts 29% facing an average of 8.4 yards.

The week-to-week story is mostly about opponents. At Tampa (now the 5th-ranked defense) he posted -12.1 EPA with a 20% bad-throw rate. Against Miami (28th) he went 27 of 37 but threw to an intended depth of 4.9 yards, took four sacks and still finished at -0.7. His accuracy is real: CPOE +3.3, 17th, and 76.5% on short throws. His aggressiveness, though, is at 7.6%, far below his 12–17% career band. His air yards to the sticks sit at -2.8, which means third downs are being played short of the marker.

The outlook darkens up front. Donovan Jackson (77% of snaps) is out with a torn meniscus, and left tackle Christian Darrisaw (89%) is in concussion protocol. A quarterback who already turns clean pockets into sacks is about to get dirtier ones. Justin Jefferson is out this week and Josh Oliver is on IR, which leaves T.J. Hockenson (+0.515 EPA per target on a team-high 18 targets) as the one reliable read. The path to a respectable season requires O'Connell to do three things: cut the screen diet, take more intermediate shots and use Murray's legs by design. Until that happens, he is a below-average passer whose team wins anyway.

strengths.title: Accurate on everything he attempts
strengths.body: His completion rate over expected is +3.3 (17th). It rises to +7.2 on throws under 10 yards, and his bad-throw rate is fifth-lowest. That fits his 2020, 2021 and 2024 seasons, when CPOE ran +2 to +4, so it is a real skill rather than a two-game heater. When he throws to someone past the line, the ball is usually where it should be.

strengths.title: Scrambles still pay the bills
strengths.body: Six scrambles have produced 41 yards and three first downs at +0.658 EPA apiece. That is the most efficient thing Minnesota's offense does. It is the same improvisational rushing that ranked near the top of the league for most of his career. The legs are intact. He has had just one designed run, so the team has more of this to unlock.

strengths.title: Downfield throws are working, sparingly
strengths.body: Intermediate throws (+0.262) and deep throws (+0.287) have both been strongly positive. Hockenson has been a clear winner at +0.515 per target. Each depth bucket is only 10 attempts, so this is a hint, not a fact. Still, it suggests the conservative play-calling is costing more than it protects.

concerns.title: Sacks in clean pockets
concerns.body: He has been sacked on 9% of dropbacks (32nd) despite one of the lowest pressure rates in the league. His 2.96-second time to throw is the slowest of his career. Poor sack avoidance has followed him every season, including a 50% pressure-to-sack rate in 2025, so this is who he is, not noise. It gets worse now that the starting guard is gone and the left tackle is in concussion protocol.

concerns.title: The screen game is a black hole
concerns.body: Nearly a quarter of his attempts (17 of 71) have come behind the line of scrimmage. Those throws average -0.616 EPA with a 12% success rate and include an interception. The problem is mostly scheme and execution: Aaron Jones is at -0.181 per target on 14 targets. It is fixable by play-calling, which makes it the most likely part of his EPA to improve.

concerns.title: Playing short of the sticks
concerns.body: His 7.6% aggressiveness is well below any season of his career, and his average throw lands 2.8 yards short of the first-down marker. On third down that produces a 29% conversion rate and -0.4 EPA per play. Some of this is the role in a run-first offense carried by its defense. But it leaves the offense unable to sustain drives, and Minnesota's success rate is last in the league.

trend.note: Week 1 lasted 17% of snaps, and he missed Week 2. The jump from -12.1 EPA at Tampa to -0.7 against Miami tracks the opponents (5th vs. 28th defense) more than any change in his play. Both full starts were below average.

nextGame.headline: Bottom-three Saints defense meets a Vikings line coming apart
nextGame.body:
New Orleans ranks 30th in defensive EPA, 27th against the pass and last in success rate allowed. It sits 25th on short throws, the area where Murray's accuracy lives and where Minnesota calls most of its passes. The Saints' pass rush is middling (18th in sack rate, 19th in hit rate), so the sacks Murray takes on his own should ease somewhat. They allow 237 passing yards a game to QBs (11th), and their league-worst run defense gives Minnesota's run-leaning plan an easy script.

Availability cuts both ways. Minnesota is without Jefferson and guard Donovan Jackson, has Oliver on IR, and has Darrisaw questionable in concussion protocol. That makes this a short-passing, Hockenson-and-Addison game behind a patched line. On the other side, linebacker Kaden Elliss (100% of snaps) and edge rusher Carl Granderson (65%) were inactive for Monday's game against Atlanta, and DT Davon Godchaux left it with a groin injury. Their status for Sunday is unclear. If Elliss and Granderson sit again, the middle of the field and the edge rush both soften. The Saints' offense is also missing Etienne, Fant and Tyson against the league's best defense.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game vs. soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Murray completes 76.5% of throws under 10 yards, and New Orleans is 25th in EPA allowed on short passes. This is where his accuracy should turn into positive plays rather than the break-even results he has had so far. It holds as long as the throws come at the line or past it, not behind it.

keyMatchups.title: Reshuffled left side vs. ordinary rush
keyMatchups.body: Jackson is out for the season, and Darrisaw's return date is only an estimate. Murray's sacks have come with little pressure, so the combination of a weaker line and his slow trigger is the real risk. A Saints rush that is only 18th in sack rate, possibly without Granderson, is the best-case opponent for that weakness.

keyMatchups.title: Game script tilts to Minnesota
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota's defense leads the league in EPA allowed. It faces a mid-pack Saints offense missing its top back, a tight end and a rookie receiver. The Saints' run defense is 32nd. Expect Minnesota to protect leads on the ground, which caps Murray's attempts but should give him manageable downs.

nextGame.watch: How many of his throws land behind the line of scrimmage, and whether he gets the ball out on third down behind the reshuffled left side.

restOfSeason.body:
His accuracy, scrambling efficiency and the run-first, defense-first context are all sustainable. That context alone keeps his volume modest, in the low-to-mid 30s for attempts in competitive games. His EPA should drift up from -0.22 toward the slightly-below-average range. The screen-game drag is the kind of thing play-callers fix, and the schedule cannot keep producing Tampa-level defenses. The sack rate is the part least likely to regress in his favor: it is a career-long trait, and it now meets a weakened line. He should take 2.5 to 3.5 sacks in a typical full game until protection stabilizes.

Upside depends on Jefferson's return and on O'Connell trusting him with more intermediate throws, which have worked in a small sample, and some designed runs. A 1.4% TD rate is too low for a quarterback with his red-zone accuracy, so passing touchdowns should tick up. The low passing volume will keep his fantasy ceiling in check.
swingFactors: Offensive line health: Darrisaw's return and Jackson's replacement
Jefferson's return from the ankle sprain
Whether O'Connell cuts screens and adds intermediate shots or designed runs

bets.reason: The league's top defense by EPA, sack rate and success rate faces a Saints offense missing Etienne, Fant and Tyson. New Orleans' own defense ranks 30th in EPA. Minnesota's offensive injuries keep this from being stronger, but a 1.5-point spread asks very little.

Minnesota's two games with Murray at full snaps produced 39 and 25 total points, both unders. The Vikings' offense ranks last in success rate and runs more than expected. Its defense should suppress a depleted Saints attack, even though the Saints' defense is bad.

New Orleans is 27th in pass defense EPA and 25th on short throws, and allows 237 yards a game to QBs. Murray's short-area accuracy fits that weakness. Jefferson's absence and the run-heavy script cap the upside.

The Saints rank last in rush defense EPA and 30th in explosive runs allowed. Murray's scrambles have averaged +0.658 EPA. A softer front, possibly missing Elliss and Granderson, should give him room when he breaks the pocket.

confidence.note: Only 84 dropbacks and two full starts with a new team. An offensive line in flux and Jefferson's absence add uncertainty.
